enonce_markdown: Let $\mathbf{P}$ be a $3\times 2$ matrix and $\mathbf{Q}$ a $2\times 4$ matrix. Which statement is correct?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The product $\mathbf{XY}$ exists only when the number of columns of $\mathbf{X}$ equals the number of rows of $\mathbf{Y}$; its order is then (rows of $\mathbf{X}$) $\times$ (columns of $\mathbf{Y}$).

### Solution

$\mathbf{PQ}$: $\mathbf{P}$ has $2$ columns and $\mathbf{Q}$ has $2$ rows, so the product is defined and has order $3\times 4$.

$\mathbf{QP}$: $\mathbf{Q}$ has $4$ columns but $\mathbf{P}$ has only $3$ rows, so it is not defined.

### Method reminder

For a $2\times 2$ matrix, $\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc$. Watch the sign when $b$ is negative.

### Solution

$$\begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 5 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 3(4) - (-2)(5) = 12 + 10 = 22.$$

enonce_markdown: The matrix $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following is $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

For $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}$: swap the leading diagonal, change the sign of the other two entries, divide by the determinant.

### Solution

$\det\mathbf{A} = 4(2) - 3(2) = 2$, so $\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \dfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$.

Check: $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\frac32 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

The other options keep the wrong signs, fail to swap the diagonal, or multiply by the determinant instead of dividing.

enonce_markdown: Find the value of $k$ for which the matrix $\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & k & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has no inverse.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A square matrix has no inverse exactly when its determinant is $0$. Expand the $3\times 3$ determinant along a row, using the signs $+\ -\ +$.

### Solution

$$\det\mathbf{M} = 1(k\cdot 1 - 1\cdot 1) - 2(2\cdot 1 - 1\cdot 0) + 3(2\cdot 1 - k\cdot 0) = (k-1) - 4 + 6 = k + 1.$$

$\det\mathbf{M} = 0 \Rightarrow k = -1$. Dropping the minus sign of the middle term would give $k + 9$ (so $k=-9$), and a sign slip on the last term would give $k - 11$ (so $k = 11$).

enonce_markdown:
The matrix $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

(a) Find $\det\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$.

(b) Hence solve the simultaneous equations $2x + y = 3$, $\ x + 3y + z = 6$, $\ y + 2z = 5$.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

$\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det\mathbf{A}}\operatorname{adj}\mathbf{A}$, where $\operatorname{adj}\mathbf{A}$ is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors. A system $\mathbf{AX} = \mathbf{b}$ is then solved by $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$.

### Solution

**(a)** $\det\mathbf{A} = 2(6-1) - 1(2-0) + 0 = 10 - 2 = 8$.

The matrix of cofactors is $\begin{pmatrix} 5 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ (it is symmetric, so it equals its transpose, the adjugate). Hence

$$\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \frac18\begin{pmatrix} 5 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}.$$

**(b)** $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} = \dfrac18\begin{pmatrix} 15 - 12 + 5 \\ -6 + 24 - 10 \\ 3 - 12 + 25 \end{pmatrix} = \dfrac18\begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 8 \\ 16 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}.$

So $x = 1,\ y = 1,\ z = 2$. Check: $2+1 = 3$; $1+3+2 = 6$; $1+4 = 5$.

enonce_markdown:
The matrix $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

(a) Show that $\mathbf{A}^2 = 5\mathbf{A} - 5\mathbf{I}$.

(b) Hence express $\mathbf{A}^3$ in the form $p\mathbf{A} + q\mathbf{I}$.

(c) Hence find $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ in terms of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{I}$, and write it as a matrix.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Compute $\mathbf{A}^2$ directly, then reduce higher powers by multiplying the relation by $\mathbf{A}$ and substituting it again. To find an inverse, rearrange the relation into $\mathbf{A}(\dots) = k\mathbf{I}$.

### Solution

**(a)** $\mathbf{A}^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5 \\ 5 & 10 \end{pmatrix}$ and $5\mathbf{A} - 5\mathbf{I} = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 5 \\ 5 & 15 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5 \\ 5 & 10 \end{pmatrix}$. They are equal.

**(b)** $\mathbf{A}^3 = \mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{A}^2 = 5\mathbf{A}^2 - 5\mathbf{A} = 5(5\mathbf{A} - 5\mathbf{I}) - 5\mathbf{A} = 20\mathbf{A} - 25\mathbf{I}$, so $p = 20,\ q = -25$. Check: $20\mathbf{A} - 25\mathbf{I} = \begin{pmatrix} 15 & 20 \\ 20 & 35 \end{pmatrix}$, which equals $\mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{A}$.

**(c)** From $\mathbf{A}^2 - 5\mathbf{A} = -5\mathbf{I}$: $\mathbf{A}(5\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}) = 5\mathbf{I}$, so

$$\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \frac15(5\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}) = \frac15\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.$$

Check with $\det\mathbf{A} = 5$: $\dfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ agrees with the standard $2\times2$ inverse.
